title: Reformster Nostalgia and New Old Mistakes
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene responds to a wave of “reformster nostalgia”—exemplified by Mike Petrilli and Rick Hess’s Ed Week conversation “Can School Reform Be Bipartisan Again?”—that mourns the lost bipartisan consensus of the No Child Left Behind, test-and-choice era. Greene rejects the diagnosis that reform faltered from “reform fatigue” or because it was “simplistic and self-righteous,” arguing instead that it flagged because it did not work: high-stakes testing narrowed curriculum, taught a generation that education means a Big Standardized Test, and mostly served data-hungry tech interests and those seeking to dismantle public education. He distinguishes the coalition’s serious wing—people he disagrees with but can converse with in good faith—from the “culture panic” crowd who replaced “competition improves schools” with “get those trans kids off the track team” and whom he judges fundamentally unserious. Greene attacks reform’s foundational premise that schools need external “pressure,” invoking Campbell’s Law against top-down accountability and “Greene’s Law”—that the market rewards superior marketing, not superior quality—against school choice, and he denies the standardized test validly measures educational quality at all. He reframes the real divide as pro- versus anti-public-education rather than left versus right, and his constructive proposal is that any revived reform coalition must seat actual working teachers (not two-year Teach For America alumni), because reform’s recurring blind spot is the reality of implementation.
points: Greene’s central counter-diagnosis: reform didn’t fade from “fatigue” or a public pendulum-swing but because its core mechanism—high-stakes testing—failed on its own terms while inflicting real damage, from curriculum narrowing to teaching students that school’s purpose is a test score.

He draws a hard line between the coalition’s “serious” members (whose values he thinks flawed but who argue in good faith) and the “culture panic” crowd, whom he casts as using words to manipulate and as interested only in cultural dominance and personal power rather than educational quality.

The piece attacks reform’s premise that schools need external pressure: top-down accountability breeds a compliance culture governed by Campbell’s Law, and market competition is a poor fit because—by “Greene’s Law”—the free market fosters superior marketing, not superior quality.

Greene treats the Big Standardized Test as an emperor with no clothes: there is no evidence that raising a student’s scores yields a richer or happier life, yet a single math-and-reading test is accepted as a total verdict on education, underwriting claims like David Brooks’s that red states are ‘beating’ blue states.

His prescription reframes the fight as pro- versus anti-public-education rather than left versus right and insists a credible movement must include working teachers, since reform continually misses the viewpoint of the people who must actually implement its ideas.
quotes: It’s not just that the ed reform movement became infected with Culture Panic. It’s that the Culture Panic crowd is, almost without exception, a bunch of very unserious people.
Fatigue? Simplistic? No, the reason that reform flagged was because it didn’t work.
Market competition is a terrible fit for education (see Greene’s Law-- the free market does not foster superior quality; the free market fosters superior marketing).
There isn’t a shred of evidence for that assertion, but in the meantime, we keep pretending that a single mediocre math and reading test tells us everything we need to know about education.
Did test scores go up for a while? Sure. I was there. They went up because we learned how to align the schools to the test. Not to the education-- to the test.
I think it’s more accurate to frame the sides as pro- and anti- public education, and pro-public education voices have always been in very short supply in the reform coalition.
But ed reform continually misses the viewpoint of the people who have to actually implement policy ideas.
